subsubtopic: CONTROL OF GASOLINE PRICES-EFFECT OF ACTION BY COMPANIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek the unanimous consent of the House pursuant to Standing Order 43. The urgency and pressing necessity of this matter arises, so I am informed, from present and combined activity by some, perhaps all, of the major oil companies to change thousands of contracts with retail gasoline outlet dealers. The new contract provides that ownership of all gasoline delivered by these distributors to the retail dealers will remain with the distributors instead of the retailers. This means that control of consumer prices for gasoline will shift from the retailer to the supplier. With present concern over the cost of living at the stage where price controls may be necessary, the effect of such private and concentrated control over the price of a product that is a necessity to millions of Canadians requires action by this House. With unanimous consent, I would therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser):
That the matter hereby raised be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and that it be an instruction to the committee to report back to this House as quickly as possible with its recommendations.

subtopic: MONTREAL OLYMPIC GAMES, 1976-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MONTREAL OLYMPIC GAMES, 1976-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are aware of all the attention which this government brings to the financing of the Montreal summer Olympic Games of 1976.
More than four years ago, this government has clearly defined its position, namely that we would not make any special financial contribution to these games. In letters dating as far back as 1968 and since then, on the occasion of numerous public statements, Mayor Jean Drapeau has indicated that besides certain current federal-provincial programs, no financing was required on the part of the federal government.
While the organization of the games is the responsibility of the City of Montreal, the federal government has taken an interest in them by reason, on the one hand, of the international character of the undertaking and, on the other hand, of financing methods considered by the City of Montreal and the Olympic Games Organization Committee (COJO).
In fact, hon. members know that on announcing its $310 million budget last week, COJO proposed that except for the amount of $18 million, the total revenue expected be provided through fund-raising programs.
Although such programs are intended for the Canadian and the foreign public at large rather than the federal taxpayer as such, nevertheless they require the approval of federal authorities.
Besides the expenses covered by the City of Montreal budget, we must also expect that the Canada Olympic Games will cause disbursements for the various federal departments in the discharge of their usual responsibilities.
We are considering two main points: First, the government seriously wonders whether COJO can balance its budget. In November last, we received a copy of that budget and according to the appraisal conducted by federal officials, a deficit can be expected.
Mr. Speaker, may I stress that this is our own point of view. I know that the Quebec government and the Montreal municipality probably hold different views, which I respect. As concerns the cost of an event that belongs to a still distant future, of course, a possibility of disagreement exists but, as I said, we fear that a deficit might occur and this is one reason among others why we have taken precautionary measures with which I will deal in a moment.
Secondly, we fear that some unexpected contingencies might cause a considerable increase in the cost of the games, for this happened on the occasion of previous

February 2, 1973
The Olympic Games
Olympic Games and of Expo 67. This is why we intend to do everything possible to help the games' organizers maintain the cost at the lowest possible level, as they themselves have stated they will.
Such, then, are the main facts that led to my statement before the House last week, to the effect that we wanted assurance that, if there were a deficit, it would be made good by a body other than the federal government. This guarantee was to my mind essential if parliament was to be called upon to look into the action suggested by COJO with regard to plans to secure funds, plans that the City of Montreal calls plans for self-financing, which are more likely to call upon the general public than on the taxpayer as such.
Mr. Speaker, the government has now received a letter from the Prime Minister of Quebec containing a clear assurance that his government would not seek financial assistance from the federal government should a deficit arise.
The government has also received letters to the same effect from the city of Montreal and from COJO. With the permission of the House, I should like to table these letters now. The government considers that the agreements by Premier Bourassa in his letter, and by Mayor Drapeau and Mr. Rousseau in theirs, provide the assurances we have sought. Since we believe a deficit is a clear possibility, these assurances are important. These letters guarantee that any deficit would not be laid at the door of the federal government.
The government is now willing to act upon the request of the city of Montreal and COJO concerning the special issues of Olympic stamps and coins. And we are continuing discussions with the government of Quebec, the city of Montreal and COJO on the best way of answering COJO's request for an annual lottery.
Before I conclude, I would like to make very clear the nature of the federal outlays that may be involved in meeting the requirements generated by the Olympics for normal federal services. As I indicated earlier, these are not included in the budget presented by COJO.
One large cost item is the Olympic village. Between
2,000	and 3,000 dwelling units are contemplated. Funding by CMHC could range from $26 million to $54 million, depending on the number and costs of the units and the amount of commercial financing. We feel it is quite reasonable to consider that this could be handled between now and 1976 under the normal CMHC allocations for public housing, which go out to all provinces, since the share which has gone to the province of Quebec has been running at some $100 million annually. After the games, the Olympic village would become part of Montreal's housing stock.
Second, we must recognize that the large influx of Olympic participants and spectators will put particular pressures on various services which in the very nature of things would have to be provided by the government of Canada, such as personnel from the RCMP, the Canadian armed forces and customs and immigration. It is obvious

that if the Olympics are held in Montreal, as they will be now, the federal government cannot stand aside and say: "We will not be involved in questions of security or customs or immigration." Yet, these are implied costs in the sense that they would not have occurred had the games not taken place. We anticipate this might involve some $20 million in increased costs, and we are determined to maintain a strict control over such costs.
Finally, there is a further cost increment which would be incurred if the CBC assumed the role of "host broadcaster" providing the basic television service at the games. In this event, net costs to the Crown corporation would be an estimated $25 million. Discussions are continuing on whether the CBC would or should undertake this function, and naturally the government will have to reach a decision in that regard.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has a strong and legitimate concern over arrangements for the 1976 Olympics. This concern does not, however, diminish the warm welcome which will be extended to the Olympic games and its participants by the government and by Canadians generally. It is a challenging undertaking and I am sure that all Canadians wish it well.

subtopic: MONTREAL OLYMPIC GAMES, 1976-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MONTREAL OLYMPIC GAMES, 1976-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by using the words with which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ended his statement, that this is a challenging undertaking, one that all Canadians wish well. Speaking on behalf of my colleagues and myself, I can say that we certainly wish it well and we wish to be co-operative.
I must say that I have some concern following the Prime Minister's statement. One reason, though not the only one, why I wish the games well and wish to co-operate is that I believe that Canada's good name, as well, of course, as the good name of Montreal and the good name of the people of Quebec, is involved in this enterprise. I point out that in 1969 the Prime Minister wrote a letter to Mr. Brundage of the International Olympic Committee in which he said:
The government of Canada warmly supports the application of the city of Montreal for the honour of being host to the 1976 summer Olympic games. I therefore offer you a hearty welcome and extend to all who are associated with the Olympic games a cordial invitation to visit us in Montreal in 1976.
At that time the Prime Minister made it clear within Canada that the government was not committing itself to direct grants to support the Olympic Games, but I believe the international Olympic community and other countries would be justified in feeling that the government of Canada was going to see that these games were warmly supported, were going to come off and come off satisfactorily and in a creditable way. I think I must also say that following that letter I do not believe that the Prime Minister has discharged his responsibility in allowing things to drift along the way they have drifted. So we have been confronted with this last-minute emergency, and a decision as to what we should do to make it possible for these games to be arranged and in fact take place. I have to say, Sir, that we have no firm assurance today that everything has been arranged.
February 2, 1973

It is true that the Prime Minister has received an assurance from the Prime Minister of Quebec, and I believe from the Mayor of Montreal and others, that the government of Canada will not be called upon to pay any deficit. But the Prime Minister has not received any assurance from the Prime Minister of Quebec that the province of Quebec is prepared or able or is undertaking to underwrite any deficit, or to give any assurance that in fact any finances will be provided if some of the Prime Minister's fears become realities and a deficit does become clear and looms very large. I emphasize that the Prime Minister has not arranged any assurance that this kind of situation can in fact be met. The guarantee and assurance from the government of Quebec do not amount to any such assurance. I think the House and the people of the country should understand that.
The Prime Minister has not given us any details this morning as to the proposals relating to coinage and stamps. In fact, I have to say that I have had no discussion with the Prime Minister about any of these matters except what I have heard here in the House, although I have been filled in by the mayor of Montreal and the COJO people in particular before Christmas, as a matter of fact as fully as I required, about their proposals.
I believe that how these coinage and stamp transactions are arranged is important. I believe it is important that the proceeds of the sale of the coinage come into the usual hands and that we do not get into the position where we are minting coins for an organization other than the government, however worthy that organization may be. It may well be that this is all going to be arranged through the Bank of Canada and that the bank will receive the proceeds from the sale and remit the difference between the cost of minting and the sale price to COJO. I would regard that as the correct procedure, but I presume legislation will be required to enable it to be done. Of course, it might be argued that this amounts to a grant, but I would regard it as preferable to simply minting the coins and turning them over to COJO or any other organization at mint cost. This, I think, would be a grave departure from our established traditions and procedures. I assume, as I say, that legislation will be introduced and, if so, we will want to examine it. We will also be concerned about the manner in which the stamps are to be handled.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I have to point out that although the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has received an assurance that his government or the government that may succeed it-the government of Canada, to be nonpolitical-will not be asked to cover any deficit, he has not in fact received any assurance, except from the city of Montreal, about the actual financing of the games. I think I heard that the provincial treasurer of Quebec say that the Quebec government is prepared to meet a deficit of $5 million to $10 million. The House should understand there is no assurance that, if the games run into heavy weather between now and their opening, the government of Quebec will put up more money. I say that for clarification.
I think it is very important that the country as a whole be involved in these games, Mr. Speaker, and support them.

Mr. Speaker, my party welcomes the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today in which he took some trouble to outline the parameters of federal involvement in Canada's first Olympic games. We wish our first Olympic games every possible success as a potentially great moment in the history of our nation.
We in the New Democratic Party, however, are not unmindful of certain criticisms and reservations that have been expressed about the games not only in Canada but in many other quarters. We have heard that the Olympics are not truly amateur in nature, that the recent games were far too costly, and that there are many other priorities for funds in this troubled world faced with problems of poverty, overpopulation and pollution. We have heard also that the games have been potentially too nationalistic in nature. Many other reservations have also been expressed. We hope, therefore, that the Montreal committee will be conscious of the original traditions of international athletic events and not turn the Montreal games into an extravaganza. We look forward to Canada leading the way in staging the games on such a budget scale that, in future, developing countries in Asia and Africa can also afford to act as hosts to the games.

Mr. Speaker, my party approves the concept of the issuing of special coins and stamps. We appreciate the assurance of the Prime Minister and of the Montreal committee that the people of Canada will not be asked to pick up any deficit. The Prime Minister himself has assured us that under no circumstances will Canadians be asked, through the federal government, to finance any deficit that may possibly accrue from the games. I will not emphasize this point because the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) spent considerable time in discussing

February 2, 1973

the matter in greater detail. We welcome the Prime Minister's assurance.
I now wish to mention our concern about federal involvement through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I think it is opportune to raise a couple of points at this time. First, we believe that housing for the Olympic village funded through existing and proposed programs under the National Housing Act must be of such design as will meet the objectives under which those programs have been funded. We feel that the needs of the future occupants must be considered first, and not the temporary needs of visiting athletic contingents. The second point is that grants and loans similar to those made available to the city of Montreal through existing or proposed federal programs ought to be made available concurrently to other cities on a pro rata or population basis.
We suggest that if the coming event is to be justified from the standpoint of broad national interest and support it is essential that Canadians, above all, not be denied the opportunity to view the games in their own country. We recommend that tickets for prime events be distributed on a population basis. Between 10 and 20 per cent of the tickets for seats for prime events ought to be sold to average Canadians throughout the provinces and not sold in blocks to large dealers and corporations for them to give away as tax-assisted favours. We feel that the seats should go to the population at large as it is the people of Canada who will be asked to support the games.
Finally, we hope that the Olympics in 1976 will mark an end to some of the unfortunate trends evident in recent Olympic games and that the world athletic community will embark on a new Olympic spirit in Montreal, a spirit reflecting what is best in the Olympic ideal, a spirit that will rekindle interest and acceptance not just by the affluent industrialized nations of the world but also by the developed and developing nations which, together, make up the rich mosaic of our planet. We welcome the athletes who will visit Canada, many of whom will be visiting this country for the first time, and hope it will be a tremendous experience for them as they pace one another on the road to athletic excellence.

Mr. Speaker, it would have been surprising to see the Canadian government ignore an event which interests all nations. So we were happy to see that a decision has finally been made on the subject, for a somewhat unhealthy atmosphere was starting to build up around that issue. There seemed to be a morbid fear that the country would be called upon to participate financially in that event which is of international scope. This is why one could perhaps be inclined to taunt the government with not having moved quickly enough.
Mr. Speaker, one had to be careful about the fertile imagination of Mayor Drapeau and his propensity for spending and I think that the final decision is good not only for the City of Montreal, Quebec and all the rest of Canada but that it will also show the whole world that
Canada knows how to do things and it is for us a reason to rejoice.
A column in yesterday's La Presse suggested that this method of financing could well be considered by many as stemming from Social Credit. Mr. Speaker, I wonder if that might not bring the government to examine further what Social Credit actually is.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry. Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
that Bill C-3, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very happy occasion for me when introducing my first legislation before the House of Commons. I think that the House should also be gratified with this legislation. We have moved early in this session, and in a positive way, to support the growth of Canadian jobs.
In my speech on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne I anticipated the amendments which are before us this morning. I stated that we would be bringing in further measures to increase the capitalization of the Export Development Corporation and to raise the financial ceilings for lending, guarantees, export insurance, and foreign investment insurance operations.
These amendments deal with the financial ceilings for lendings and guarantees. They do not deal with the other matters referred to in my earlier speech. At a later stage I would hope to introduce amendments dealing with export insurance and foreign investment insurance operations, and a number of other technical and housekeeping amendments.
I believe hon. members will find these amendments to be brief, simple and straightforward, and in my remarks I intend to be brief, simple and straightforward.
Let me introduce the subject by going back through the history of this act which, in my view, was one of the most successful acts of the 28th parliament. The original Export Development Corporation Act was passed in 1969. At that time it replaced the former Export Credits Insurance Act, the ECIC Act.
The ceiling in the original act passed in 1969 was $600 million for direct loans. Two years later in 1971 this was raised to $850 million, indicating the rapid growth in the financing of capital goods and related services by the Export Development Corporation.
I would like to emphasize that these loans are made not to Canadian exporters but to the buyers of Canadian export capital goods and related services. The loans are made to the buyers rather than the vendors.
The growth, as I have indicated, has been dynamic. In the early 1960's we were averaging something in the order of $50 million to $60 million of placements each year under the predecessor act. With the new Export Development Corporation Act the loans in 1970 increased to $96 million, nearly double the average of the previous several years, and since then they have continued to build.
Financing agreements signed by the Corporation with foreign buyers of Canadian goods and services rose

February 2, 1973
Export Development Act
dramatically, as I say, in 1970 to $96 million, in 1971 to $240 million, and in 1972 to $283 million. This might be translated as well in terms of jobs. All members of the House are concerned with the provision of jobs. As I said in my speech during the throne speech debate, the present level of the outstanding loans, $700 million, has the equivalent value in jobs of about 100,000 jobs. This dynamic growth is continuing and the prospects for 1973 are considerable. Based on requests currently under consideration by the corporation they may well exceed about $500 million; under the existing long term lending and guaranteed ceilings the Export Development Corporation has the capacity to sign agreements for over $200 million to provide for these requirements. This, then, is the background to these amendments, Mr. Speaker.
The details of the amendment I think I have already indicated-raising the loan ceilings from $850 million to $11 billion and consequential amendments with respect to the capitalization of the corporation which provides for ten times the capitalization. That is to say, Mr. Speaker, the loan ceilings are related to ten times the capitalization of the corporation.
The export demand that I have referred to-this dynamic growth-should be seen alongside the export performance of the Canadian economy over the last four or five years. There was an increase between 1969 and this year of roughly $5 billion-from $14.9 billion to $19.9 billion. I think the important point with respect to the financing of the Export Development Corporation is that it is geared to and directed to capital goods, high technology and labour intensive projects. In other words, it is a major contributor to helping Canada diversify its exports from reliance on crude and unprocessed materials to the more sophisticated, more fabricated, more fully finished goods that we are anxious to promote. The expansion has been remarkable and I should like to give some examples of the industries that have been supported under this plan and the markets that have been purchasing Canadian goods and services under this particular provision.
A list of the projects shows steam generators for Mexico; turbines for Brazil; locomotives for Greece and Turkey; electrification equipment for Mexico and Brazil; a zinc and lead refinery for Turkey; telecommunications to the Philippines; hydro-electric project for Brazil; an airport project for Israel costing $10 million; locomotives for Yugoslavia; pulp and paper project for Kenya; a chemical plant for Yugoslavia costing $21 million; mining equipment, iron pelletizing for Peru and Argentina and an order for railway boxcars for Zambia. I would be pleased to provide the details of the amounts of these projects in Committee but I thought it might be a help to give the background of the kind of financing to indicate the markets and projects supported.
These loans are only granted to a foreign buyer in respect of Canadian capital goods if there is an 80 per cent Canadian content in the order which the foreign buyer seeks. The underwritings are arranged through export development offices in Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto and in other centres through the offices of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Generally speaking, these loans would be for something over five

years and under 15 years at rates of interest competitive with those offered by other countries. I should like to emphasize that, Mr. Speaker, because other countries are offering this kind of supportive financing to their industries. At the same time, I should like to make it clear that Export Development Corporation loans do not compete with the private sector-indeed, they support the Canadian commercial banking institutions.
Mr. Speaker, I said that I would be brief and straightforward. I do not believe that on second reading I need to go into very much more detail as we will have opportunities for that at the committee stage. However, I should like to emphasize the point that I have already made: this is not an effort to compete in the sense of undercutting other types of financing activity but to support the commercial lending practices internationally, to support our exporters, to help them meet, in addition to questions of quality, price, service and delivery dates, the competition of other international financing agencies in support of their country's exports.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that hon. members should find these amendments controversial. I hope they will consider them quickly so that we can get on with the job of supporting Canadian export industry, thereby supporting the growth of Canadian jobs.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the face of it, Bill C-3 appears to be a very simple bill. The operative sections merely increase the capitalization of the Export Development Act from $75 million to $125 million and the loan limit under section 30 from $850 million to $1.5 billion. Actually, however, the issues are much more complex than the bill indicates. To investigate each aspect of the operations of the corporation would require more time than is available today. Consequently, I shall just content myself with a few preliminary remarks and suggestions and leave more detailed examination to the committee stage where my colleagues and I will have the opportunity to question directly the officers and directors of the corporation and to inquire into its activities and philosophy more comprehensively.
At the very outset, Mr. Speaker, the question arises as to why the bill is presented in this form at this time. The minister has just advised us that he proposes to introduce amendments to other sections of the act at an early date. We are at a loss to understand why, in that case, the whole package was not presented to us simultaneously.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
The only apparent reason for this omission is the suggestion that the loan limit under section 30 has already been exceeded in fact. At least that would be the case if guarantees already signed are taken up. It appears obvious under the circumstances that the only reason the government is presenting the bill in this narrow form is in the hope of easy passage. They hoped that once again they could get away with something. They hoped that Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition would not find out that they had exceeded the authority given them by parliament. They hoped that once again they would evade the charge
February 2, 1973

that they are both extraordinarily bad planners and contemptuous of parliament.
If indeed this is the case, Mr. Speaker, there is no reason in the world why the government could not have anticipated the necessity of the increased loan limit last summer. It would have been a very simple matter to have introduced this kind of bill during the brief session in September. In the circumstances existing at that time, the full co-operation of all opposition parties would have been cheerfully given in expediting the bill. Having missed this opportunity, either through carelessness and bad planning, or else through a deliberate attempt to avoid getting into questions of this kind which might have opened up the Unemployment Insurance Act as well, the government waited until the situation had reached crisis proportions. It is a habit which is occurring all too regularly. The government is taking on the characteristics of a punch-drunk conglomerate staggering from crisis to crisis.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION

speechtext: Even in view of these extraordinary circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we have no intention of obstructing and filibustering.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Go on!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: We are always constructive and helpful.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
I wish to serve notice, on the other hand, that we intend to pursue a full and complete examination of the philosophy and the operation of the corporation. Anything less would be unworthy of us as an opposition, and certainly not in the best interest of Canadian exporters and taxpayers.
The theoretical rationale of this act must clearly be that the encouragement of exports is an obligation upon the body politic and that the sort of machinery provided by the Export Development Corporation Act will fulfil that obligation. Yet surely the purpose of exports, the real rationale for policies of this type, is more complex. First, we sell abroad in order to achieve economies of scale. We want to make our manufactures and capital goods more competitive in domestic as well as in foreign markets. Second, we wish to earn foreign exchange in order to pay for necessary imports, both capital goods and current consumption. Third, we wish to help, to the extent that exports are a stimulus, Canadian firms develop and maintain the leading edge of technology. Fourth, we wish to assist foreign countries in some cases by the provision, on terms acceptable to them, of our goods and services. Fifth, and high on the priority scale in the minds of Canadians, we export in order to provide jobs for Canadian workers.
There is a widespread belief that it is necessary to export in order to achieve full employment at home. One
Export Development Act
must entertain this thought with caution, however, because it represents a considerable carryover from the economic thinking of the 1930's. More current economic philosophy would hold that it is possible to attain full employment domestically regardless of the level of exports. In other words, the total level of employment is a function of aggregate demand in Canada, and if the same amount of credit that we intend to make available for the finance of exports were made available to Canadians, for similar purchases, the net effect on employment in Canada would be the same. If this is so, then it should be borne in mind in our analysis of the philosophy and success of the Export Development Corporation and in our evaluation of priorities in the use of available credit.
In considering the philosophical and operational guidelines which might be taken into account, a number of questions arise. Are we making too many long-term loans, for example? Is it possible that we have been moving too quickly and too far in this direction? Would it be more advisable to concentrate to a greater extent on short and medium-term loans in order to achieve a faster turnover? Would this in the long run be more beneficial to Canadian taxpayers?
Should the Canadian commercial banks be allowed to participate more fully? Until the end of 1971, all capital required for the corporation's spending operations came from the Consolidated Revenue Fund; but with the requisite approval of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the corporation has since attempted to borrow the money commercially. How successful has it been? The minister neglected to inform us on that question this morning. The former minister of industry, trade and commerce said in February of last year that he expected, with a little moral suasion, the chartered banks would participate to the extent of $100 million in 1972. Was that goal achieved? To what extent has the corporation been able to cut down the calls on its own capital by arranging loans in concert with the banks? To the extent that the banks have participated, has this in all cases been on a last-in, first-out system whereby the bank advances its share at the last possible moment and is repaid first? If so, how is the system working? Certainly, in establishing guidelines we should consider the alternative uses of available credit.
In January, 1972, the EDC basic scheme of insurance was extended to the giving of unconditional guarantees for specific loans made by banks to exporters for the production of capital goods for export on medium-term credit. Similar guarantees may now be given to banks in respect of obligations issued by the foreign buyer. These new guarantees apply to both goods and services and they are of significant assistance to consultants, design and managerial businesses. As to manufacturing, the result is that EDC has stepped from the post shipment risk to guaranteeing loans for actual production.
While it may be argued that this is a logical extension of the facilities of the Export Development Corporation, it should be noted that the same terms and conditions are not available to those who sell domestically. It may be thought that tariffs, anti-dumping duties, quotas, and so on, are the domestic equivalent of the financial assistance given to exporters. On the other hand, it can be strongly argued that if there is an international competitive war in

Export Development Act
the concessional financing of the export trade, exports will aid the foreigner perhaps at the expense of the domestic consumer. How many Canadian producers of domestic products and consumers would be elated at the prospect of obtaining financing on the same favourable terms and conditions that they help to make available to foreigners through the Export Development Corporation?
Perhaps a more representative board of directors would help to weigh these questions more objectively. With the passage of the Export Development Corporation Act in 1969, representatives of the business and exporting world were induced to serve on the board of EDC along with members of the public service. Originally four, the outside representation has since been increased to five and the public service representation reduced to seven by an amending act of 1971. I would like to see the balance between the public and the private sectors at least reversed. Certainly, there is no requirement for seven civil servants. Half that number could ably represent the government's point of view. Freeing the others to concentrate on their primary responsibilities would certainly help to expedite the decision-making process in government. At the same time, the representation of the private sector could be increased in such a way that small business could be more adequately represented and greater diversification of interests be included in the nominees. I would hope that the government would agree to an amendment along these lines when the bill is considered at the committee stage.
Notwithstanding any changes which might be contemplated by the board of directors, it is still the responsibility of parliament to give guidance in respect of a number of important guidelines. Among the philosophical issues that we should discuss and express an opinion on is the desirability of Canada ensuring private investment in the less-developed countries. Is this kind of assistance really welcome in the host country? Should some form of domestic participation be required? Will the concern in these countries develop along the same lines that our concern in Canada has developed as the breadth and depth of foreign ownership of our industries and resources have increased? A government might welcome the investment despite the fact that opprobrium for Canada might still result among the citizenry. This is more than an academic question. It is a fundamental aspect of Canadian foreign policy which should be discussed and on which direction should be given to the corporation.
One of the most important policy guidelines which should be given the corporation by parliament is the extent to which the corporation should continue to finance the exports of foreign-owned Canadian industries and of foreign branch plants in Canada. In reviewing the operations of the corporation to date, one cannot help but be struck by the extent to which the Canadian taxpayers' money is being used to subsidize exports from foreign-owned industries situated in Canada. A very sizeable proportion of the total credit has been used in this direction. The long-term significance cannot be underestimated.

What if the Burke-Hartke Bill is passed and becomes law in the United States? Will jobs then be repatriated
from Canada to the United States, notwithstanding the fact that the companies have enjoyed over a long period beneficial use of the Canadian taxpayers' money? Or even if the bill is not passed, and if some of the more contentious aspects of the bill are not incorporated in administration bills, and I am optimistic enough to think that we can persuade the Americans that it is not in their best interests to proceed, are we still not putting ourselves in an unnecessarily vulnerable position by making too large a proportion of our credit available to American and other foreign subsidiaries? It is worth noting that in the long-run, this policy produces less net inflow of foreign exchange which is one of the purposes of our export policy. To the extent that interest, dividends and royalties flow out of Canada in the direction of the head office of the corporations, our exchange position is worsened.
While it would probably be irresponsible to suggest an abrupt change in the existing patterns, I think it would be equally irresponsible not to demand a shift in emphasis. More credit should be made available, both in relative and absolute terms, for the export of Canadian manufacturers produced by Canadian-owned companies. This would give Canadians the extra benefit derived from the leverage accruing from this kind of loan. It would enable us to put fewer eggs in one basket. It would allow us to reduce our dependency on changes in policy outside our country which might affect employment inside our country and over which we have no control. Firm guidelines should be established because Canadians have the right to know that their credit is being used in a way which will maximize the long-term benefit to them as citizens and taxpayers. My colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) who will speak next for the official opposition, will develop this argument in greater detail.

The other area where urgent change is required is in the amount of effort and credit made available to small business as a proportion of that made available to big business. The allegation is often heard that corporations cater to large businesses and ignore the small. This appears to be particularly true in the export financing division where as the Financial Post, January 20, 1973, states:
On average most contracts are for five or more years and valued at more than a million dollars.
Such allocation of funds makes it difficult for smaller companies to get their share of the action. The Export Development Corporation 1971 annual report illustrates this factually. The finance agreements signed from January 1, 1971 to December 31, 1971, totalled $240,034,634. Of this the smallest loan was made to the Dominion Road Machinery Company Ltd., for $225,255. More typical is the size of loans given to companies such as H. A. Simons (International) Ltd. $12 million; Marine Industries Ltd. $43 million; Telecommunications and Equipment Services, $6,329,353; MLW-Industries Ltd., $7,575,025; Davie Shipbuilding Company Ltd., $14.5 million and so on. The corporation is big business oriented and apparently does not have the facilities or inclination to service small business adequately. Noteworthy in this context is the fact that

speechtext: I recall the experience of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) when he was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He travelled across the country to tell small businesses that they should take advantage of the credit facilities that were available to them for exports. Many of them tried and had their application rejected. The then minister had to laydown the law and the corporation responded. Loans to small business enterprises increased dramatically.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Obviously, the aversion is deep-rooted and some radical change is necessary. The solution appears to be a new, small business section dedicated exclusively to the service of small business. It should be established as a matter of urgent priority. It should open regional offices in each district of Canada so that the small businessmen who are unable to afford the time and expense to come to Ottawa would be able to service their requirements close to home.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Once the system was functioning adequately, briefings could be given to small businessmen in each district. They should be encouraged to use the facilities to the maximum extent possible and to expand their activities on an international scale. The results would be dramatic. The whole world would become the oyster of Canadian small business. To achieve this, however, would require a much more energetic and aggressive approach than has been achieved to date. There has been too much centralization in Ottawa. There has been too much concentration on the big deals and too little time and credit left for the average entrepreneur.
In summation, Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to do an objective evaluation of the success of the corporation to date. Most of the large exporters are quite well satisfied with the experience so far. Most of the small manufacturers, on the other hand, are less than satisfied. The popular press is quite optimistic and gives the corporation full marks. Certainly, if the criteria is spending money, they have done well. A dramatic increase in outstanding loans and commitments has gone a long way toward overcoming the attitudes expressed in 1969 that the Exports Credits Insurance Corporation had been excessively cautious and somewhat unmindful of the increase in assistance given to their exporters by other industrialized nations especially Japan and Western Germany.
How far have we gone in catching up? How are we doing in comparison with other countries? How far have we yet to go? These are some of the questions that will have to be answered.
It should be understood, of course, that this bill in itself, regardless of the guidelines that are applied, will not solve all of the problems of Canadian business, especially small business. Our tax laws, our death duties, the attitude of our government toward business in general, our financial
Export Development Act
institutions and the facilities available to Canadian businessmen are all amongst the questions that will have to be addressed. They are, in total, far more important than the bill we are now discussing.
But in so far as the Export Credit Act is concerned, it is obvious that we have come a long way in three years. Equally obvious, there is still room for improvement. The operations of the corporation can be more Canadian, more selective and, above all, more compatible to the needs of Canadian small business enterprises.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, the principle of it, certainly is really quite a good example of what John Kenneth Galbraith meant in his book, "The New Industrial Estate", by the partnership between government and private industry. It is usually the kind of partnership in which the government takes most of the risks and private industry receives most of the benefits.
The opposition is trying to embarrass the government because of the success of the Export Development Corporation. It is obvious that the requests reaching the corporation are beyond its financial ability to meet at the moment, and parliament is being asked that the ceiling be increased. I believe we should agree to these increases. However, there are some questions which ought to be asked about the whole concept of the development corporation as presently set up.
What it is, in our view, is largely a defensive reaction against what has been going on in virtually every country in the world. If anything, we were late in getting into the field. We found that in international markets other countries were subsidizing their exporters with various insurance projects, underwriting certain costs at interest rates lower than were available at any other source. Canada felt it had to get into that business. For a long time we were experiencing a great deal of difficulty in this country as a result of what is sometimes called the concessional financing of other countries. We ran into a situation in which we gave large grants under DREE or some other program to a province or to an industry, only to find that Canadian industry had been outbid or underbid by an offshore bidder. This was not necessarily because the Canadian price was higher or conditions were different; it was because the offshore bidder had arranged for special financing which made it more profitable for a Canadian buyer to buy offshore than domestically.
There were two directions in which we could have moved. We could have been tougher on this concessional financing and kept those goods out of the country by applying regulations against dumping, or finding some

February 2, 1973
Export Development Act
way of obliging them to offer terms in Canada on the same basis as they offered terms in their own country. The government chose not to take that approach. Instead, it said: All right, if they are doing it to us we shall go out around the world and meet five with five. It is an interesting question whether we ought to have proceeded along these lines. I think that in the interim, because this country does not have a real industrial strategy, or a real industrial development program, we probably had no choice but to take the course which was followed. Having said this, I believe a heavy responsibility still rests on the government to deal with concessional financing as it is applied to Canada.
I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). He said we go to great lengths to sell our products around the world yet we often lose out in our own domestic market. This is the case. We often lose orders in the domestic market as a result of concessional financing arrangements of other countries. I am not at all sure that the hon. member for Trinity really had much of value to contribute to the debate. I listened carefully to him, hoping that he would come up with some ideas which would change things. But I did not find any. I was interested in his comments about the need to get the banks, or private investors, involved. That is not going to happen until such investors can look forward to a much greater return on their money than is possible under the system set up by the Export Development Corporation.
The Export Development Corporation has in fact become a lender or an insurer of last resort. It exists because of a failure on the part of private banks and money institutions. If the marketplace were working as well as my hon. friends to the right would like to think, there probably would not be a need for an Export Development Corporation. The point is that it is not, and the government has had to step in and make up for the inadequacies of the marketplace.
I always believe there are some valuable functions that can be performed by the government, and, therefore, we acknowledge the necessity of what is being done rather than try to be cavalier about the situation.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: That is pretty cavalier.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
There is in existence a myth that we have to export everything in order to increase our balance of payments position, but very seldom do we hear the question raised as to whether we have to export as much as we do. Very often the consequence of exporting as a total policy is that we get into somebody else's market on a basis of concessional financing, and those people in turn do the same thing with us. The situation was reversed in this case because they started and we followed suit.
We had a minister of industry, trade and commerce at one time who never really understood the relationship between exports and imports. He was always congratulating himself and his government for having increased exports by some 16 per cent, for example, and would then follow up by saying that he had some bad news to report, that we also increased imports by 16 per cent. He could never see the relationship, or that you cannot export with-

out importing for any period of time unless there is an adjustment in the dollar value or a compensation by way of inflows or outflows of capital. Over any period of time, exports and imports tend to balance each other.
What is really important about this relationship is not the amount of exporting we are doing, but the kind we are doing and whether it is beneficial to the country as a whole. Fortunately, I think most of the projects financed by the Export Development Corporation seem to be of a beneficial nature, particularly to industrial production in this country. Even then, some questions have to be asked about these things.
Let us consider the shipbuilding industry as an example. A great deal of the underwriting in respect of ships has been on offshore sales. What is of interest is that shipbuilding is one of the most heavily subsidized industries in this country. It may be that we have to subsidize the shipbuilding industry, but we find we then have to underwrite its sales and its financing around the world. At some point someone has to question whether in terms of the kinds of things we are doing we are gettirtg much benefit from the shipbuilding industry, or whether this is highly desirable for Canada. We recognize that shipbuilding is centred in those areas where there is high unemployment and that we must maintain a reasonable level of employment there. To the extent there is no other industrial structure in these unemployment areas we probably have to continue this shipbuilding program, but as we look into the future we must ask ourselves whether we want to expand this program, particularly when there is so much risk and so much public money going into its support and development.
Another aspect can be found in the Export Development Corporation annual report. It contains a beautiful picture of a swimming pool beside a little hacienda on one of the Caribbean Islands. It contains a statement to the effect that we are helping to build or finance this. Is this the sort of thing the Export Development Corporation should be getting into with the taxpayer's money? It is one thing to say we are selling certain materials internationally and supporting these sales with finances because this provides employment opportunities in Canada, but what kind of employment opportunity does the financing of summer resorts in the Caribbean provide Canada? This may provide some profit for enterprising Canadians, but on the whole it does not seem to be of any great value to the Canadian public generally. As such, I do not think this should be underwritten by a public corporation. If there are Caribbean countries which want Canadian support, this might best be provided under CEDA rather than under a program of this kind. I am a little concerned that we may be following the path, albeit this is a very small step in that direction, which we deplore other countries following. It is a kind of imperialistic move into areas in which we may not want to be in the future.
There is a great deal of unrest in many developing countries about their land being bought up by foreigners, and there is a great deal of hesitation about their future desire to see this type of development. I do not think Canada should be involved in that kind of development, and it should not be aided and abetted by Canada unless there is a specific request from the governments of those
February 2, 1973

countries for support of this kind. I would be much happier to see us support the government operations of those countries to develop the land under their own ownership and management. As a Canadian I would feel more comfortable about that, and I think most Canadians would feel the same way.
There have been allusions and much talk about industrial strategy. The government claims it has been caught up by an industrial strategy of some kind. If it has, this strategy is almost invisible and very ill-defined. Like so many organizations, the Export Development Corporation is operating in a kind of a vacuum or an absence of stated policy as to what the government is trying to do and what are its objectives. The government seems to be responding to the problems of concessional financing, but it is difficult to see this in the context of future strategy.
Some of the things being supported have a great deal of value to Canada, but there are some things that do not seem to relate to anything that has been carefully thought out for our future. Recently the government undertook a review of foreign policy and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) issued a statement which made reference to three options for Canada. It seems he was in favour of the third option.
The first option was to continue drifting, as we have been doing, although the minister did not put it in those words. That seems to be out of the question because the world is not going to let us drift. The second option seemed to involve a continental arrangement with the United States, but there is much public opinion against this. The minister seemed to say that this would not work and, therefore, we are left with the third option. That option was to develop some kind of policy for Canada which would make us more independent and our markets more accessible and, in some way, make us less reliant on foreign trade and international changes. We have seen very little effort in this direction by the government.
Admittedly, the government recently introduced a bill on foreign ownership which makes some move in the direction of future industrial planning, but again even that is not in any framework or context that is understandable. 1 suggest we must have some indication from the government of what its long-term plans are. I am not talking about rigid long-term plans; there is no such thing as an inflexible long-term plan for any country. Rather I am referring to some statement of principle as to how the government will respond in the future to the challenges around the world, such as to the fact that we are being cut out of the European Common Market, that the United States market is becoming more protectionist, that Japan really wants to buy only our raw materials. Increasingly, we are finding ourselves placed in an isolated position and we are badly in need of an over-all review of the industrial future of this country. An industrial future can only be realized if the government takes a definite stance and makes some plans, prepares priorities and outlines to the country the desirable direction in which we should be moving.
I was also interested in the comment of the hon. member for Trinity who expressed concern about multi-
Export Development Act
national corporations. He said that the Export Development Corporation tends to support very heavily these international corporations and he would like to see more Canadian companies receive help. What I was waiting for him to say, but which never seemed to emerge from his statement, was that at some stage he was going to move an amendment excluding foreign held corporations from the benefits of the provisions of the Export Development Act. In the absence of that kind of suggestion, it is difficult to measure just how serious is the Canadianism of the hon. member for Trinity.
We do face a dilemma here, a challenge between the multinational corporation and a particular government, in this case the Canadian government. The multinational corporations have been using Canada in the same way as they have used every other country in the world. After all, they could just as easily export from Italy or France as from Canada. Multinational corporations ask Canada what kind of deal we can give them, and they indicate to us that the Italians have given them one deal and that they can get a better deal from the French; that the Germans have offered them so much concessional financing, and they ask us what we will put up. This country has never tried to grapple with the problems posed by multinational corporations. We have to establish an Export Development Corporation to match what other countries are prepared to offer. This is a nice arrangement for the multinational corporations, since they can hop around the world from one country to another getting the best deal they can. But I am not at all sure that is ultimately to the best benefit of Canada, except only in the most indirect way.
Therefore, while we have probably no choice at this time but to go along with and support something like the Export Development Corporation, since it does help in maintaining and keeping employment in Canada, I suggest it is not the most useful mechanism for the future. The most useful tool for the future would be giving greater government attention to the development of an industrial strategy to find some sense of purpose and control over our economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-3 entitled an Act to amend the Export Development Act.
Mr. Speaker on many occasions a similar bill was introduced, mainly to increase the credits, the funds of that corporation and to find ways of increasing our exports.
Mr. Speaker, since we have to actually subsidize exports there is surely something which is not working properly in the export-import system. Surely, there are questions to be asked. For example, why do foreigners hesitate to import Canadian products? Do they have doubts on the quality of our products or do they consider our prices prohibitive? I think that in the final analysis it is our prices which are slowing down our imports. This is due to our overall cost system which is related to our tax system at all levels of Canadian production. This results in almost prohibitive prices for our products not only for export but also for domestic consumption, to the point where competition with other countries is becoming more and more difficult.

February 2, 1973
Export Development Act
In our export system the objective of the government seems to be mainly to export unemployment because we see that all the means used by the government to stimulate exports seem to be aimed at having industries operate fully to ensure employment for Canadian workers. This seems to be a good guideline but it is the worker who through the taxes he pays is partly financing government grants to stimulate exports, and so he is really the one who is paying to work.
In this country, we have been taught that we must export or die. Mr. Speaker, I think the principle of exports should consist in compensating for imports, nothing more. Our policy should be aimed at insuring production, at facilitating the finishing of raw materials and at encouraging as much as possible domestic production of consumer goods. I think we have a tremendous domestic market and I wonder whether we are developing it properly. I think that before attempting to encourage exports and foreign consumers, we should rather try to encourage Canadian consumers in order to enable them to use our own production for their own needs.
There is one particular method to achieve this objective. It would consist in granting a compensating discount on all Canadian products used in this country. This would enable us to use a good part of our production at the expense of import markets.
This would also increase production. It would enable our factories to produce more, and at the same time it would satisfy the Canadian consumer.
Trying to export means to some extent trying to export our unemployment. What we make for export will not be made in other countries, and so it is we who are working instead of others. When we import-for you cannot export all the time, you have to import too-the opposite takes place; we import unemployment.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I call on the government to seek a policy that will enable us to produce at home the consumer goods we need, and to promote this production by every available means so that it may reach the consumer. The aim of production, whether agricultural or industrial, is consumption.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the few remarks I wanted to make about the bill now before us. I admit that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce requires further estimates to encourage even more exports. As long as we operate under the present system, I suggest that there may be no alternative. I think that we should get off the beaten tracks and find another way to meet at the same time the Canadian worker is and the Canadian consumer's needs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
present bill which will augment advantages under the Export Development Act is one which I support wholeheartedly. The whole idea of increasing our trade with other countries is, of course, vital to the life of Canada. It means that what it takes to enhance our exporting is the difference between what one government can do as opposed to another or what certain individuals can do as

opposed to certain other individuals, and this is one means that we have at our disposal to improve the export picture of Canada. There have been many occasions when I have visited other countries and when we have spoken about exports the idea of financing became a stumbling block. Certainly, experience has shown us that if there are competitive financing methods available in the international market, exporters will be able to do business much more easily.
I remember, for example, that a year and a half ago I was in Leningrad on a short visit and had the opportunity of meeting the pulp and paper people there. It was certainly a joy to me that, prior to that occasion, we had passed amendments to this act which facilitated further business with the Soviet Union in the field of pulp and paper. At that time the Soviets were negotiating for a very large new pulp and paper complex, and the help that Canada was able to give was beneficial, not only to them, but to Canadians because they insisted on using a Canadian company. Even though their principal consultants were a French firm, they insisted on the involvement of a certain Canadian company and we were able to discuss with them the possibilities which were enhanced through this act.
I think that everyone in the House is probably generally in favour of this act. It is a question of certain details being clarified. Various parties perhaps have different ideas about these details, and certainly it seems to me that the government is wide open to accepting suggestions from various people.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer)-for whom I have great respect and admiration-spoke this morning on the subject and made a couple of observations. In one instance he referred to the economic theory that if the same financing were available to Canadian industries, the end result by way of the creation of jobs would be the same as under the present system where the financing is available from abroad, and therefore jobs are created within Canada in order to fill those contracts. The hon. member did not say whether or not he espoused that theory as opposed to the other one, but he brought it forth as a cautionary measure in order to make us aware of the fact that this is an alternate theory which we should consider. Personally,-and I am certainly no economist-I do not think that that particular theory is valid, because when we provide this kind of financing to foreign governments to buy from Canada or to develop through the use of Canadian goods and talents, we are providing not only jobs here but also that other element in trade which is necessary. It puts the other country in the position of being willing to do more business with Canada when more goods are purchased from Canada because trade is always a two-way street. I suggest that when we take these steps in order to help another country, that country is better disposed to do more business with Canada. Therefor, I think that the comparison of the net results on a job for job basis is not valid, because there are other factors that are involved.
The hon. member also mentioned the fact that exporters are given advantages that are not available to other businessmen in Canada who are interested in the domestic market. This is true when we are talking about this par-
February 2, 1973

ticular bill, but it seems to me that other facilities are available to those who are interested in the domestic market. I come from an area which is very anxious to expand its industrial base, an area that is trying very hard to develop secondary industry in particular. We do have the facilities available to help these other domestic companies. Certainly, whether the program under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has or has not been effective, is another question. It is certainly there and available. Our problem has not been that these companies have not had something at their fingertips that they can use. Our problem has been that we have not been able to convince these people that it is more advantageous for them to go into these areas than into others.
The hon. member mentioned something else, with which I certainly agree wholeheartedly, namely, the matter of the composition of the board. This is a favourite subject of mine. The hon. member has suggested that the number of civil servants on the board should be reduced and that there should be other people-perhaps businessmen-who should be included instead. I could not agree more because, first of all, I think it is absolutely essential that people who deal with business matters should have a background in business.
I have seen so many instances of companies, in my constituency and elsewhere, which have been waiting for the government to make a decision, even though it may be a minor one. Probably the employees within the bureaucracy left that file in a basket over night, or while they went away on holiday, or while they were off sick, and all the time, each and every day that the file was there, it cost the company money. These people, although very efficient-I don't downgrade them-do not realize what it is to meet a payroll at the end of the week, or to meet such other problems as are related to dealing with the employees of companies. Therefore, I agree wholeheartedly that a minimum number of civil servants should be put on the board, and that generally its composition should be made up of business people who are familiar with the world of business.
Of course, I return to my old argument that there should be some representative on such a board from the people of Canada, or somebody who has a mandate from the people of Canada. We have lots of people in this House who have ample experience in business and who would be able to contribute. The hon. member for Trinity is an ideal example of someone who would be able to contribute that kind of experience and enhance the composition of the board.
The hon. member also talked about industries in Canada that are foreign owned, and suggested that the subsidization of these companies should be regarded with a jaundiced eye. This, of course, caught the attention of our friends in the NDP, who picked it up immediately. This subject has arisen frequently, and it is something that can be dealt with in another way. I would remind hon. members that we will be talking about foreign ownership when dealing with a separate bill entirely. It is an issue that can be dealt with separately.
Export Development Act
I have never been afraid of foreign ownership in Canada. I have been afraid of foreign control. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, it is up to us as legislators to make sure that the laws are such that there is not control by a foreign power in Canada. I come from an area that does not disdain foreign ownership, simply because we know that probably most of Northern Ontario would not even exist without that kind of foreign investment. But that does not mean to say that we can allow foreigners to control our destiny.
Some of the help that we give to other countries has been badly interpreted by many Canadians. The kind of things suggested by the provisions of this bill are badly understood by Canadians in general. That is unfortunate. It is our fault, and not only that of members of the government. Members of the House on both sides have a duty to explain to the people of Canada what our legislation is all about.
For example, people will come up to me and say that this is the kind of thing that has to do with foreign aid. This is not directly foreign aid, Mr. Speaker. It is not foreign aid at all. Yet people time and time again come along and say, "This is foreign aid. You are giving it away. Why don't you do something for our poor people at home?" That is a fine argument for someone who is concerned only with cheap political advantage, but it certainly is not the way to be sincere with the people of Canada. So far as that goes, foreign aid itself has been badly explained, because certainly any time we help anyone else in the world it is also to our advantage.
Here we are, one of the richest countries in the world-I would certainly say the most advantaged country in the world, if not the richest. We have the potential to become the richest in the world. We have every possible advantage, but sometimes we take the attitude of a cheap country cousin who says, "There are many people who are poor in our own country. We should be helping them first." Of course, we should be helping our poor people, but we should also be helping people in countries far less fortunate than ours, not only from the point of view of morality but also from the point of view of good business. When we are helping other people, we also help ourselves. When we help other people through this kind of bill, we are helping them to do more business with Canada. We are helping to create more jobs in Canada, and this is the thing we want for Canadians.
The spokesman for the Creditiste party mentioned that our Canadian consumers should be helped first. Of course, we should be trying to help Canadian consumers and there are many ways in which they can be helped, but one is not by criticizing a bill such as this. There are other ways in which we can help the Canadian consumers.
I suggest that every time we talk about our poor people at home and our "bonnes meres de famille", who have large families and so on-I am No. 14 in mine and I know about this-it is great stuff on the hustings and great stuff in the local paper back home. However, let us not forget that when we help other people through a bill such as this we create jobs and increase Canadian production, and this is indirectly helping every "mere de famille" in Canada. This is what we should not forget, and this is what should be explained to the people. We should not

have this kind of superficial thinking that instead of giving a loan to somebody outside Canada the money should all be given to the mothers of Canada. That kind of thing is ridiculous. Really it is a partisan political argument. It should not be used. We should be above that kind of thing in this House.
The hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) also suggested that by importing we also import unemployment. Surely, he isn't serious! When we import sugar from some country which grows sugar cane, does that mean we are importing unemployment? Mr. Speaker, we import coconuts; we import oranges and other citrus fruit. Does that mean we are importing unemployment? Canada lives by trade. We export what we do best; we import what we cannot grow here or what we cannot develop here. So, this kind of an argument is hardly-

-content with the markets it has had in the United States and elsewhere. To get it to expand its markets is like pulling teeth. I have been trying for five years to get the pulp and paper industry of Canada to establish markets in other parts of the world, to establish joint ventures and new markets on a longterm basis. What is the attitude of the government? I think it is very interesting when we come to consider what steps have been taken directly to help small business. Look at the Industrial Development Bank. Granted, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is not with us today, and that bank answers directly to him. But I would point out that there are some interesting contrasts to be drawn between the operations of the IDB and the operations of the Export Development Corporation.
Let us start with rates. If you go to the IDB you will be quoted rates as high as 11 and 12 per cent, should you be lucky enough to be offered a loan. In the EDC it is about 7 per cent. Now turn to loan levels. The IDB is making loans at a level of $45,000 on average. The Export Development Corporation is making loans on average of over $10 million. What a contrast to see what can be done in the name of foreign financing and what can be done in the name of financing relatively small business in this country. Again, it is interesting to find that while the Export Development Corporation finances indirectly some 30 or 40 corporations in this country, the Industrial Development Bank has somewhere around 16,000 customers.
I would strongly recommend that in working out an industrial strategy, something which the government has failed to do to date, hon. members opposite should take a much closer look at ways in which the Export Development Corporation can fit into such a strategy and see whether the corporation cannot play a much larger role in two main respects, that is, in helping Canadian small

businessmen get into or expand in the export field, and in counteracting the growing volume of foreign investment in this country.
I cannot agree with those who argue that we should endorse this type of proposal without giving the matter much more thought and closer investigation. We are being asked to lift the ceiling to $1.5 billion in favour of a Crown corporation without even having an audited statement. I hope it will sink into the minds of every member of this House that the last audited statement from the Auditor General of Canada for this corporation is dated December 31, 1971.
What would happen if any concern in the private sector tried to raise a few thousand dollars publicly in the absence of an audited statement or a prospectus? Yet we are expected to give second reading to a bill in the absence of an audited statement to the end of the corporation's last fiscal year. I would point out that not only is the ceiling to be raised, but the minister has in his possession a forecast showing where the money is actually to be spent in 1973 and 1974. He has in his possession a document showing how some of the $600 million extra money which will be within the $1.5 billion is earmarked. Two hundred and forty-three million dollars go out in 1973, and $401 million in 1974. I think we are entitled to an explanation as to why there has been such anticipation of the action to be taken in this parliament. Rather than an audited statement, we have been provided with a series of boasts from various ministers and officials that the longterm financial section of the EDC is having a fabulous time and is a great success.
I assure the minister that if he went outside parliament today with a bag of candy and offered it, he would get rid of it just as he has been getting rid of some of his longterm favourable financing at 6 per cent to 8 per cent. I should also mention that in delivering his argument the minister was in many ways serious in general, but in substance I do not feel that he put sufficient emphasis on the serious request he is making of this parliament. Longterm viable banking institutions do not stand on whether they can get money out, but whether they can get it back; and the viability of a public institution is not that it can disperse public money, but that it disperses public money in the public interest.
Long-term foreign financing is a risky and a costly business. A case has been made that public money should be used in this area because the private sector is unwilling to do the job. I am not certain that is the case. However, there are ways in which the public could be more active in this area, and I would suggest that the Export Development Corporation has not prudently explored this field.
